title: Writing an Airflow DAG That Can Be Re-run Safely
intro: mlops-tutorial-014 operated Airflow. This is the author's side. A DAG is a Python file that declares tasks and their order; most pipeline trouble is decided when it's written: whether a re-run duplicates data, whether a year of history runs by accident, whether one slow file slows every other DAG. You've written dags/daily_orders.py, with the DAG id daily_orders.

steps.prompt: The cheapest test first: does the file import at all? Run it with Python.
steps.fake_output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "dags/daily_orders.py", line 4, in <module>
    from pandas import read_sql
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'
steps.explanation: The file fails on an import: pandas isn't installed where the scheduler runs.
steps.why: A DAG file is just Python, and the scheduler imports it. If the import fails, the DAG never appears, with no error anywhere a user would look. Running the file directly takes a second and catches syntax errors and missing packages. Heavy imports at the top of a DAG file are a cost as well: the scheduler re-parses every file constantly, so import libraries inside the task function that needs them.

steps.prompt: With the import moved inside the task, the file loads. Show the DAG's tasks as a tree, to check the dependencies are what you intended.
steps.explanation: extract, then transform, then load. And notify stands alone, depending on nothing.
steps.why: notify was meant to run after load and is unconnected, so it would fire at the start, announcing success before any work is done. Dependencies are declared with '>>' (extract >> transform >> load >> notify), and a forgotten link doesn't raise an error. Print the tree whenever you change the structure.

steps.prompt: Run the whole DAG once, locally, for the logical date 2026-10-01, without the scheduler.
steps.fake_output:
[2026-10-02 15:02:11] INFO - Running task extract for 2026-10-01
[2026-10-02 15:02:14] INFO - extracted 41,204 orders for 2026-10-01
[2026-10-02 15:02:14] INFO - Running task transform
[2026-10-02 15:02:19] INFO - Running task load
[2026-10-02 15:02:22] INFO - loaded 41,204 rows into warehouse.orders_daily partition 2026-10-01
[2026-10-02 15:02:22] INFO - Dag run in success state
steps.explanation: All tasks ran in order, in one process, for that date.
steps.why: 'dags test' runs a full DAG run in the foreground, so you can debug a pipeline like a script. The date argument is the logical date: the day of data the run is for, which each task receives. Tasks must use it, never the current time: a run for 1 October executed on the 5th must still process the 1st.

steps.prompt:
The DAG has start_date 1 January 2025 and a daily schedule. When it's first switched on, what happens with the default setting catchup=True?
  a) It runs once, for today
  b) The scheduler creates a run for every day since the start date: over 600 runs, started as fast as it can
  c) Nothing until tomorrow
  d) It fails to load
Type the letter.
steps.hint: Airflow tries to 'catch up' on every interval it thinks it missed.
steps.explanation: Hundreds of historical runs, all at once, unless catchup is False.
steps.why: This surprises nearly everyone once: enabling a new DAG and watching it launch a year and a half of jobs against the source database. Set catchup=False unless you really want history, and backfill deliberately with a command when you do. Also give start_date a fixed date: a start date computed from 'now' moves every time the file is parsed, and the DAG never runs.

steps.prompt:
The load task appends the day's rows to the warehouse table with INSERT. The run for 1 October fails half-way and is retried. What's in the table afterwards?
  a) Exactly the right rows
  b) Some of 1 October's rows twice: the first attempt's partial insert plus the retry's full one
  c) Nothing
  d) Only the retry's rows
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
not idempotent : INSERT INTO orders_daily SELECT ...            -> a retry adds the rows again
idempotent     : DELETE WHERE day = '2026-10-01'; INSERT ...    -> or overwrite that day's partition, or MERGE on a key
steps.hint: Retries and backfills run the same task for the same date more than once.
steps.explanation: An appending task duplicates data whenever it runs twice.
steps.why: Every scheduler retries, and every pipeline is eventually backfilled, so a task must be safe to run any number of times for the same date. The patterns: overwrite the date's partition, delete-then-insert in one transaction, or MERGE on a unique key. This one property is what makes pipelines operable; dataeng-incident-001 is what happens without it.
